title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Forwarding the Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade's 'Several Issues to Note Concerning the Implementation of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods'
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice Forwarding the Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade's "Several Issues to Note Regarding the Implementation of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods"

Fa (Jing) Fa [1987] No. 34

To the Higher People's Courts and Intermediate People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; all Railway Transport Intermediate Courts; and all Maritime Courts:

Given that the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods will become effective for China on January 1, 1988, we hereby forward to you the Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade's "Several Issues to Note Regarding the Implementation of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods." Please organize relevant personnel to study it carefully so as to correctly implement the Convention in foreign-related economic trial work. If any issues arise during implementation, please promptly report them to this Court.

Attached: Several Issues to Note Regarding the Implementation of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods

December 10, 1987

Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade

Several Issues to Note Regarding the Implementation of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods

(87) Wai Jing Mao Fa Zi No. 22

To the Departments (Commissions, Bureaus) of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade, Foreign Trade Bureaus (General Corporations) of all provinces, autonomous regions, municipalities directly under the Central Government, and cities with separate planning status; all general corporations; and all industrial trade corporations:

The Chinese government formally ratified the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (hereinafter referred to as "the Convention") on December 11, 1986. Given that more than 10 countries have acceded to the Convention, it will enter into force on January 1, 1988. To facilitate the correct implementation of the Convention by all our foreign economic and trade companies, we hereby notify you of the following issues to note:

1. The countries that have currently acceded to the Convention, besides China, include the United States, Italy, Zambia, Yugoslavia, Argentina, Hungary, Egypt, Syria, France, and Lesotho. In 1986, the total volume of import and export trade between these ten countries and China reached USD 9.23 billion, and the number of trade contracts was considerable. Since the Chinese government has acceded to the Convention, it has also assumed the obligation to implement it. Therefore, in accordance with Article 1(1) of the Convention, for contracts for the sale of goods concluded between our companies and companies from the above-mentioned countries (excluding Hungary) on or after January 1, 1988, if no other choice of law is made, the relevant provisions of the Convention will automatically apply to the matters stipulated in the contracts, and any disputes or litigation shall also be dealt with according to the Convention. Accordingly, companies should consider applying the Convention to ordinary contracts for the sale of goods. However, companies may, based on specific factors such as the nature of the transaction, product characteristics, and the country involved, reach contract terms inconsistent with the provisions of the Convention with foreign parties, or expressly exclude the application of the Convention in the contract and instead choose the domestic law of a certain country as the applicable law for the contract.

2. The Convention applies only to the sale of goods. The Convention adopts an exclusion method to define the scope of goods (see Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention). Goods not falling within the scope of exclusion under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention are within the applicable scope of the Convention.

3. The Convention does not provide for all laws governing the resolution of contract disputes. Our trade companies should, based on the specific circumstances of each transaction, either make clear provisions in the contract for matters not covered by the Convention, or choose the domestic law of a certain country to govern the contract.

4. Although the agreement trade between China and Hungary constitutes the sale of goods, it currently does not apply the Convention and remains subject to the "Common Conditions for Delivery of Goods" signed between China and Hungary in 1962.

5. The Convention provides for the procedures for contract formation and the rights and obligations of the buyer and seller. These provisions differ in many respects from our current laws and the customary practices of our companies. Please pay attention to these differences.

Provincial departments (commissions, bureaus) of foreign economic relations and trade and all foreign trade general corporations and industrial trade corporations should promptly and conscientiously organize foreign economic and trade cadres to study and research the Convention. Issues arising during the study should be resolved by consulting with the relevant departments, or may be reported directly to the Department of Treaty and Law of the Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade.

December 4, 1987
